newsitem.title: USA: Odds against U.S. getting Saudi barley business.
newsitem.headline: Odds against U.S. getting Saudi barley business.

text.p: Logistics and price have restricted the United States from getting a significant piece of a large Saudi Arabia barley contract, U.S. exporters said.

Saudi Arabia was seeking barley at a tender which opened on September 20 and although the result has yet to be confirmed, reports suggested it has bought 1.4 million tonnes of barley for October to December delivery.
The European Union, which enjoys a supply and freight advantage over other suppliers, may take the lion's share of the business, exporters said.
The rest could go to Turkey, Australia and Canada and little, if any, to the United States, U.S. exporters said.
"Everybody is assuming that the bulk of the grain will come out of the European Union because of the world price structures," one U.S. exporter said.

He noted it would be difficult for the United States to get barley into the pipeline, "given the amount of time it takes to move it from North Dakota to an export point to make the arrival times. December delivery in Saudi Arabia equates to November price in the U.S.," he said.
It would also take a drop in U.S. barley prices for the United States to get business from Saudi Arabia.
"Current U.S. offers are in the mid- to high-$120.00 a tonne FOB," he said of quotes in the Great Lakes area.
"That is the (price) indication that people would be willing to sell U.S. barley. Obviously, nobody is anywhere close to buying those numbers from us," the exporter said.

A second U.S. exporter agreed. "U.S. barley prices are still not competitive in the world market. We have to go down another 10 to 20 cents a bushel," he said. Barley is currently about $2.20 a bushel (FOB, North Dakota), he said.
He said he does not expect the United States to gain very much from the Saudi sale but on the other hand, he does see Canada getting a little bit of business.
"We have heard rumors that 125,000 tonnes of Canadian barley was done and that is not a very good number at all," the said.
But one Canadian exporter doubted that any Canadian barley was sold at all to Saudi Arabia, at least for now.
Saudi Arabia bought the grain at prices ranging from $146 to $158 per tonne, including cost and freight, European traders said.

"We heard anything between $158 a tonne for the nearby positions to $148 for the deferreds. The Canadian Wheat Board had only grain available for the later position which is December 15 arrival and basis the prices as we see it, it was likely the Board did not sell anything," he said.
The price they offered looks to be at a premium to the selling price," the exporter added.
The CWB had no official comment. "Anything that deals with commercially sensitive sales information, we will not confirm or deny," said Deanna Allen, communications officer with the CWB in Winnipeg.

But the exporter noted that somewhere along the line those two cargoes will be sold. "They (CWB) offered two cargoes one at 75,000 tonnes and another at 50,000 tonnes," he said. "It is a small amount of barley on a large tender and we clearly have a large barley crop in Canada," he said.
